segments.text: Math is the magic that powers artificial intelligence.
However, we interact with these systems using everyday words, which requires a specialized
translation process to bridge the gap between language and calculation.
You type a question asking for the best Avengers movie and get an answer back in complete sentences.
Since AI models process data using math, there's an invisible step happening here.
Let's see how typed letters convert into computed numbers.
The most intuitive way to do this would be to assign a unique number to every single word
in every language.
You could build a massive digital dictionary where typing a word instantly maps to its designated
numerical code.
But that system fails almost immediately.
People constantly invent new slang, misspell things, string together emojis, and write
computer code.
Even a database of a million words wouldn't be large enough to cover every sequence of
characters a person might send.
A fixed dictionary of whole words is too rigid.
To process human language reliably, AI requires a system that is modular enough to handle
any text you throw at it.
Instead of trying to memorize every whole word, AI uses reusable pieces of text called
tokens.
You can think of them as the building blocks for language.
This diagram illustrates how tokens work.
The full collection is the model's vocabulary.
Tokens are often fragments.
Take Unbelievable.
The AI constructs it from three pieces, Un, Belie, and Vable.
The real advantage is reuse.
That single Un piece is recycled to build words like Unmatchable and Unusual.
By combining these smaller fragments, the AI's vocabulary stays incredibly efficient.
It has the building blocks to interpret newly invented words, without needing a unique database
entry for every possible combination of letters.
Before you ever type a prompt, engineers decide how text will be split apart.
They analyze massive collections of written material to establish this vocabulary.
These vocabularies are incredibly extensive to handle global language.
ChatGPT's vocabulary holds about 200,000 specific tokens,
while Gemini's holds roughly 256,000.
Once the vocabulary is set, every single token in that list is assigned a specific number.
This number is its token ID, and it acts exactly like an address in a filing system.
This graphic shows the strict three-step sequence that occurs when you hit send.
First, you type your text.
Second, a program called a tokenizer breaks your text down into its reusable chunks.
Third, the tokenizer looks up the specific token ID for each chunk.
This step is purely mechanical.
Converting the written word cat into ID 4719 just identifies the text string.
It tells the AI absolutely nothing about fur or whiskers.
The token ID simply locates the piece of text in the vocabulary.
The AI extracts the actual meaning much later.
This board breaks down edge cases to show how text is fragmented.
Notice a single word often spans multiple token IDs.
We saw unbelievable break into three chunks, and basketball splits neatly into two.
Proper names do this too.
ChatGPT splits into three individual pieces.
Now, look at the fourth example, iHeartAI.
Pause and guess the total tokens.
The answer is three.
Tokens frequently group a leading space with the symbol that follows.
The SP label highlights this.
The tokenizer doesn't insert it.
Finally, an entire web address shatters into eight distinct pieces.
Absolutely every character you type, a letter, punctuation mark, or blank space,
is converted into this numerical ID system before the AI can read it.
When the AI has finished its math and generates its answer,
that output initially exists purely as a stream of token ID numbers.
To make that readable for you, the tokenizer steps back in.
It takes that stream of numbers and converts them right back into their
corresponding text fragments.
Finally, those individual text pieces slide seamlessly together to form
the readable paragraphs you see on your screen.
Words become numbers.
That is the translation process that allows an artificial intelligence
to compute human language using pure math.
